sets.relationshipLabel: two counterpart approaches, side by side
sets.explanation: Coil and rotary are the two machine families, just as blackwork and color work are the two stylistic families they can produce.

sets.relationshipLabel: thing that stops the harm it targets
sets.explanation: An antiseptic exists to prevent infection, and a barrier film exists to prevent cross-contamination — each is defined by the harm it blocks.

sets.relationshipLabel: worker and the tool of their trade
sets.explanation: The tattoo artist's hand tool is the tube, just as the apprentice's practice surface is the practice skin — each worker paired with the instrument that defines their stage of the craft.

sets.relationshipLabel: a stage and the larger whole it becomes
sets.explanation: A stencil is traced first and becomes the finished tattoo, just as a small cap piece is planned first and grows into a full sleeve — each pair names a starting stage and the larger whole it can only grow into, never the reverse.

glossary.definition: A buzzing tool with electromagnetic coils that snap a needle bar up and down, the older-style build many old-school shops still swear by.

definitions.definition: A buzzing tool with electromagnetic coils that snap a needle bar up and down, the older-style build many old-school shops still swear by.
A quieter tool with a spinning motor that drives the needle smoothly, favored for a gentler, more consistent feel.
A style done entirely in black ink, leaning on bold lines and shading instead of color.
A style built from vivid inks layered together to bring shading, depth, and mood through hue.
A cleaning liquid used on skin to kill germs before and after the needle touches it.
An unwanted invasion of bacteria in a wound, the thing every clean studio works hard to keep out.
A clear plastic wrap covering surfaces and equipment so nothing dirty touches the next client.
When germs or fluids sneak from one surface, person, or tool onto another they shouldn't touch.
The skilled person who designs and inks the artwork permanently into someone's skin.
The handheld grip that holds the needle bar steady so the artist can guide it precisely.
Someone still learning the craft, training under an experienced artist before working on real clients.
A fake, skin-like sheet used for training strokes and shading before ever touching a real person.
A transferred outline placed on skin to guide exactly where the ink will go.
The finished piece of permanent ink art living on someone's skin.
A small, contained tattoo piece, often meant to cover a spot or start a bigger idea.
A large tattoo design that wraps around the whole arm, often built from many smaller pieces.
